source.title: Problems with Chinchilla Approach 2: Systematic Biases in IsoFLOP Parabola Fits
source.authors: E. Czech; Zhiwei Xu; Yael S. Elmatad; Yi-Xin Wang; William Held

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests Approach 2 on synthetic and published IsoFLOP data and reports systematic fitting and allocation errors, including how those errors change with sampling and fitting choices.
record.gate_note: The study assumes the Chinchilla loss-surface form rather than testing whether held-out pretraining loss follows power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute. It reports results on fitting that surface and forecasting compute-optimal allocations. Published exponents cited from other studies are not treated as results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study fits Approach 2 to digitized real Llama 3 IsoFLOP data and to synthetic surfaces. It shows that the inferred compute-optimal allocation depends on the fitting method, sampling grid and QC filtering. That bears directly on V7. The Chinchilla loss form, and so the power-law allocation, is assumed rather than tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors call Approach 2's biases structural, not statistical: they arise from grid width, off-centre sampling and surface asymmetry, and imply about 6.5% wasted compute ($1.4M) at Llama 3 scale, more for asymmetric multimodal surfaces. Approach 3 with grid initialisation and LSE largely eliminates the biases, and VPNLS is presented as a simpler, equally accurate replacement.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes Chinchilla Approach 2's IsoFLOP-parabola procedure, but also compares direct surface fitting and proposes VPNLS, which separates linear coefficients from the exponent search and does not use the parabolic approximation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome changes with loss-surface asymmetry, IsoFLOP grid width, constant sampling-centre offsets, compute-dependent centre drift, quality-control filters, fitting objective and parameterization, optimizer initialization, noise level, number of budgets, and points per curve.

fits_no_version.finding: Relative statistical efficiency of scaling-law estimators (VPNLS, Approach 3, Approach 2) under noise: maximum errors and variance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Direct surface fitting with variable projection estimates scaling-law exponents more accurately and with lower variance than IsoFLOP parabola fitting.

record.problems: The study assumes the Chinchilla loss-surface form. Its characterization of sampling pathologies in published studies is qualitative and the authors say those errors are difficult to quantify precisely. Several allocation-error results are from simulations; the real Llama 3 IsoFLOP points are digitized from a published figure. The paper also notes that extrapolations become irrelevant when irreducible loss dominates.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted additional Approach 3 variants and detailed per-noise, per-budget, per-point-count error breakdowns from Section 5.4 and Figures A5–A6; these were not needed to capture the reported Approach 2 bias or its dependence on fitting choices. Omitted the Chinchilla QC progression in Figure A7, which repeats the filtering comparison on another dataset.

untested.parts: All of it; the Chinchilla loss form is assumed.
All of it; no real larger-run loss is predicted and checked.
All of it; the power-law allocation follows from the assumed surface, and no real allocation trend is tested for stability.
All of it; multimodal surfaces are only simulated from published fits.
Parameter counting and training-schedule choices; curvature away from a single power law.

missing.what: Simulated Llama 3 condition: Approach 2 DCL only 0.2% at β/α≈0.97, versus 6.5% on real data
Compounding asymmetry plus offset or drift: D* errors up to about +35% on the Asymmetric surface
On the real Chinchilla dataset, log-loss vs linear-loss Approach 3 objectives give different exponents (a 0.5571 vs 0.5665); the Huber variant differs further

record.verdict_notes: A methods paper that assumes the Chinchilla surface, so V1–V3 are not tested, despite the reader linking them. Table A2's published exponents are cited results, not rows. The Chinchilla QC progression (37.9%→12.5% DCL) is declared in rows_left_out and also supports V7.

versions.untested_parts: Whether held-out language-model loss itself follows power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude; the study assumes the Chinchilla loss surface.
The study assesses extrapolated compute-optimal allocations and their losses or deadweight compute costs, not general held-out loss predictions for larger runs.
The study tests allocation-exponent inference and the effects of sampling and fitting choices, but does not establish a universal allocation trend across real training regimes.
Architecture depth, width, and other shape changes.

Whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes. Simulated multimodal loss surfaces are used to examine fitting bias, not to validate the underlying law in those modalities.
Downstream-task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

The study examines sampling-grid width, sampling-centre placement and drift, asymmetry, and fitting objectives or methods; it does not systematically vary every possible data or training-schedule choice.

rows.subject: symmetric loss surface (α = β = 0.31)
rows.operation_detail: Fit Approach 2 parabolas to synthetic IsoFLOP curves and regress inferred compute-optimal token count on compute.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal token allocation exponent b and intercept recovery
rows.note: Reported relative errors are +6.2 × 10−12% for b and −1.4 × 10−10% for the intercept.
rows.check: Linked to V3, but the surface is synthetic and a power law by construction, so V3 is not tested. For V7 it shows no fit-dependence under symmetric, centred, noise-free conditions.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1, Table 1; Section 4.2 confirms perfectly centered, noise-free sampling.

rows.subject: Chinchilla loss surface (α = 0.34, β = 0.28)
rows.operation_detail: Fit Approach 2 parabolas to noise-free IsoFLOP curves and infer the power law for compute-optimal tokens.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal token allocation exponent and intercept
rows.value: Inferred b = 0.548387; inferred intercept = −0.578092; intercept relative error ≈ −4.1%
rows.note: The exponent is recovered accurately, but the allocation level is systematically shifted.
rows.check: The V2 and V3 links are wrong: this measures estimator bias on an assumed synthetic surface, not real loss extrapolation or a real allocation trend. Approach 2 shifts the intercept by −4.1%.

rows.subject: Asymmetric loss surface (α = 0.46, β = 0.15)
rows.operation_detail: Fit Approach 2 parabolas to noise-free IsoFLOP curves and infer the power law for compute-optimal tokens.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal token allocation exponent and intercept
rows.value: Inferred b = 0.750000; inferred intercept = −1.459957; intercept relative error ≈ −8.5%
rows.note: The exponent is accurate in this condition, but the inferred allocation level is biased.
rows.check: The V2 and V3 links are wrong for the same reason as r2. Intercept bias is −8.5%.

rows.subject: Chinchilla loss surface (α = 0.34, β = 0.28)
rows.operation_detail: Vary Approach 2 IsoFLOP sampling-grid width and extrapolate the inferred token allocation.
rows.measure: Relative error in predicted compute-optimal token count
rows.value: Inferred D* error increases from −0.3% on XS to −5.1% on XL
rows.note: The text states that negative errors are underestimates and wider grids amplify the error.
rows.check: The V2 link is wrong: it extrapolates an estimator on a synthetic surface. The error grows with grid width, a fitting-design choice.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2.2, Table 3 and Figure 5, Chinchilla annotations and caption.

rows.subject: Asymmetric loss surface (α = 0.46, β = 0.15)
rows.operation_detail: Vary Approach 2 IsoFLOP sampling-grid width and extrapolate the inferred token allocation.
rows.measure: Relative error in predicted compute-optimal token count
rows.value: Inferred D* error increases from −1.7% on XS to −23.1% on XL
rows.note: The text describes increasing underestimation with wider grids and greater asymmetry.
rows.check: The V2 link is wrong. The baseline is not stated for this surface.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2.2, Figure 5, Asymmetric bar annotations; absolute optimal token count is not stated.

rows.subject: symmetric loss surface (α = β = 0.31)
rows.operation_detail: Apply a constant multiplicative offset to Approach 2 sampling centres.

conditions.value: 3× the true optimum at every compute budget

rows.measure: Compute-optimal token prediction and allocation-exponent/intercept errors
rows.value: All four grid widths overestimate D*; the narrowest grid has the largest error. The exponent is recovered while the intercept is biased.
rows.note: The paper says the intercept error decreases monotonically as the grid widens; the plotted values are not transcribed here.
rows.check: The V2 and V3 links are wrong. A sampling-centre offset biases the intercept; the plotted errors are +1.5% to +4.0%.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3.1 and Figure 6: exponent preserved; positive intercept bias decreases with grid width.

rows.subject: symmetric loss surface (α = β = 0.31)
rows.operation_detail: Apply a compute-dependent multiplicative drift to Approach 2 sampling centres.

conditions.value: from the true optimum at the lowest budget to 3× the true optimum at the highest budget

rows.measure: Compute-optimal token prediction and allocation-exponent/intercept errors
rows.value: The drift affects both the exponent and intercept; the inferred allocation is biased.
rows.note: Unlike a constant offset, a compute-varying offset changes the slope of log D* against log C.
rows.check: The V2 and V3 links are wrong. Drift biases both exponent and intercept; D* errors are +1.7% to +6.1%.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3.2 and Figure 7: drift changes both exponent and intercept.

rows.subject: Llama 3
rows.operation_detail: Digitize published IsoFLOP points, fit Approach 2 allocation power laws, and compare extrapolated allocations with Approach 3 surfaces.
rows.measure: Inferred compute-optimal token allocation and deadweight compute loss
rows.baseline: Approach 3 allocation: 10.1T tokens; Approach 2 allocation: 16.1T tokens
rows.value: Approach 2 overestimates compute-optimal tokens by approximately 60%; DCL is 6.5% of the budget, reported as $1.4M
rows.note: The paper reports Approach 2 b = 0.5368, rounding to the Llama 3 paper's reported 0.537.
rows.check: On real data, Approach 2 and Approach 3 give different splits (16.1T vs 10.1T tokens). This is fit-dependence, not a test of V2 or V3.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3, Figure 1, Llama 3: Approach 3 row and accompanying empirical-data paragraph.

rows.subject: Llama 3
rows.operation_detail: Progressively apply quality-control filters to Approach 2 IsoFLOP data and compare extrapolated allocation with an Approach 3 surface.
rows.value: After all listed QC stages, DCL = 0.02% ($4.7K)
rows.note: The text attributes nearly all reduction to off-centre and weak-curvature filters.
rows.check: QC filtering choices change the Approach 2 allocation (DCL 6.53%→0.02%). The V2 and V3 links are wrong.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3, Figure 2: Raw unfiltered and final Post-QC rows.

rows.subject: Asymmetric loss surface (α = 0.465, β = 0.155)
rows.operation_detail: Compare Approach 2 exponent inference under additive Gaussian noise and drifting sampling centres.

conditions.value: 2 to 4 budgets; 4 to 32 points per curve; 256 noise realizations per configuration

rows.measure: Maximum relative error in compute-optimal allocation exponents a and b
rows.baseline: True exponents for the simulated surface
rows.value: Approach 2 maximum errors: 716% on a and 239% on b
rows.note: The authors state that the systematic inaccuracy persists even with 32 points per curve and low noise.
rows.check: Synthetic noisy exponent inference: Approach 2 maximum errors of 716%/239%. The V3 link is wrong.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.4, experimental-design paragraph, Figure 11 caption and paragraph immediately following it.

rows.subject: Asymmetric loss surface (α = 0.465, β = 0.155)
rows.operation_detail: Compare grid-initialized Approach 3 using the Chinchilla LSE reparameterization and log-loss objective.

conditions.value: 2 to 4 budgets; 4 to 32 points per curve; 256 noise realizations per configuration

rows.measure: Maximum relative error in compute-optimal allocation exponent a
rows.baseline: True exponent for the simulated surface
rows.note: The paper says typical accuracy is comparable to VPNLS, while the log-loss objective is slightly misspecified for the simulated additive Gaussian noise.
rows.check: A comparator in the study's method-benchmark; it reports estimator performance under noise, not fit-dependence of a published law.

rows.subject: Asymmetric loss surface (α = 0.465, β = 0.155)
rows.operation_detail: Compare VPNLS using L-BFGS-B with analytical gradients.

conditions.value: 2 to 4 budgets; 4 to 32 points per curve; 256 noise realizations per configuration

rows.measure: Maximum relative error in compute-optimal allocation exponents a and b
rows.baseline: True exponents for the simulated surface
rows.value: Maximum errors = 34% on a and 11% on b
rows.note: VPNLS has the smallest maximum errors in this comparison, but the errors are not zero.
rows.check: The study's own method (VPNLS) compared with others; this should not be a result row.

rows.subject: symmetric loss surface (α = β = 0.31, A = B = 400, E = 1.69)
rows.operation_detail: Compare estimator variance for recovering the compute-optimal exponent b under Approach 2, Approach 3, and VPNLS.
rows.measure: Variance of the estimator for b
rows.note: The paper summarizes Approach 2 as having roughly 8× higher variance than Approach 3 or VPNLS, even under these ideal conditions.
rows.check: Reports estimator variance in the unbiased setting, a statistical-efficiency comparison rather than a dependence of the split on fitting choice.

relationships.condition: Real Llama 3 IsoFLOP data, plus synthetic or published-surface simulations with asymmetry, wide grids, or off-centre or drifting sampling
relationships.reason: Approach 2 vs Approach 3 differ by about 60% in tokens on Llama 3 (r8); QC choices move DCL from 6.53% to 0.02% (r9); synthetic biases appear in r2–r7 and r10–r12.
relationships.display_finding: Approaches 2 and 3 differed by about 60% in Llama 3 token allocation, quality-control choices moved DCL from 6.53% to 0.02%, and simulations showed sampling-dependent biases.

relationships.display_finding: Approach 2 recovered the true exponent and intercept exactly; simulated Llama 3 with β/α≈0.97 also had only 0.2% DCL.

tranche.reason: The study identifies structural biases in a widely used allocation estimator and shows that allocation prescriptions require qualification by fitting method, sampling design and quality-control choices.

source_check.notes: Llama 3 optimal allocations and DCL are estimates conditional on fitted surfaces, without independent training validation. The source inconsistently reports simulated Llama 3 DCL as 0.2% ($39K) in prose versus 0.1% ($25K) in Figure 1; neither discrepancy affects the listed rows.
